Tell me about yourself..answer: I'm a software engineer with about four years building distributed systems and data pipelines across finance and supply chain, and the thread running through my work is making large-scale systems reliable and fast for the people who depend on them. I started by co-founding a startup, Al-Shala, where I built an MVP on AWS for over a thousand concurrent users, so I learned early what it means to own something end to end. At Blue Yonder in Bengaluru, the work I'm proudest of was rebuilding a pipeline that took about ten days to build datasets, with volume growing past 80 million records a month. The hard part wasn't the code — it was earning trust. A senior colleague was worried a rewrite would silently corrupt the numbers, and honestly that pushed me to be more rigorous than I'd planned. I [ran both pipelines in parallel and diffed the output] until we both agreed it matched, then redesigned it around Kafka and Snowflake and brought it from ten days to under eight hours. That taught me that correctness has to be provable, not just claimed — a lesson I carried straight into JPMorgan, where I now architect and own a validation agent in our Software Factory platform. It checks generated code against a Jira ticket's acceptance criteria and feeds structured feedback into self-correction loops. I built it precisely because I'd learned not to trust output I couldn't verify. It's cut manual developer intervention by 90% and sped up Close of Business reports by 70%, with zero audit failures in APAC reporting. That's why Google appeals to me — doing exactly this, at the scale where billions rely on it.

followUps.q: You said a colleague's doubt changed how you worked — did you ever get it wrong before that?
followUps.a: Yes. Earlier I'd shipped a change at Blue Yonder confident the output was right, and [a small subset of records didn't reconcile] after rollout. It wasn't catastrophic, but it was my miss, and I owned it to the team that day. That's exactly why the parallel-diff habit stuck — I'd rather over-verify than ask people to trust my word. It's the same instinct behind the validation agent now.

followUps.q: You've only been at JPMorgan about a year — why leave so soon?
followUps.a: I'm leaving towards something, not away. I've learned a lot about building AI agents safely in a regulated setting, and I'm grateful for it. What I want next is to do this reliability and data work at Google's scale, where systems serve billions, with a stronger engineering culture around me. The thread's the same — I just want a bigger canvas for it.

followUps.q: When your validation agent and a developer disagree about whether code is correct, who wins?
followUps.a: Neither automatically — the point is to surface the evidence. The agent compares code to the ticket's acceptance criteria and returns structured feedback, so the disagreement becomes concrete rather than a matter of opinion. If the criteria themselves are ambiguous, that's a signal the ticket's underspecified, and I'd go back to the author. For regulatory logic I keep a human in the loop on top. That's how we held zero audit failures.

How do you handle negative feedback? Giv.answer: I treat negative feedback as someone showing me a blind spot, so I try to understand it before I react. At Al-Shala, which I co-founded, my co-founder pushed back hard on how I was building our live trainer sessions. I'd gone deep on WebRTC streaming quality, and he told me flatly I was over-engineering it while trainers were waiting on the scheduling and subscription flow they needed to get paid. My first instinct was that streaming was the hard part and the rest could wait. But instead of defending it, I asked him to walk me through what trainers were actually saying — and the complaint was that they couldn't reliably book a session at all, so streaming quality didn't even matter yet. He was right. So I owned the re-sequencing end to end: I paused the streaming polish, shipped the meeting-scheduling algorithm and the subscription model first, then came back to streaming. Before that, bookings were failing often enough that trainers couldn't depend on the platform; afterwards we launched the subscription revenue model, supported 1,000+ concurrent users, and lifted internal operational efficiency by about 20% off [that broken-booking baseline]. That reach mattered beyond us two — it's what let trainers actually earn on the platform. The relationship got stronger because I'd taken his view seriously rather than as an attack. What I learned is that feedback about priorities stings more than feedback about code, because it means I was busy on the wrong thing. So now I check my sequencing against real user pain early — I carried that straight into how I prioritise work at JPMorgan.

How do you handle negative feedback? Giv.why: The question is explicitly about receiving negative feedback, and S8 is the one setting where a peer's challenge changed the candidate's mind and they can honestly say the other person was right.

followUps.q: Was there a moment you thought he was wrong — how did you handle still disagreeing?
followUps.a: Early on, yes — I thought streaming was our differentiator, so rather than conceding on instinct I asked him to walk me through the actual trainer complaints. Once I saw they couldn't even book, the evidence settled it and I dropped my position. I'd rather be shown I'm wrong quickly than argue from my own assumptions, so I asked for evidence instead of pushing back.

followUps.q: How do you make sure you're not just agreeing to avoid conflict?
followUps.a: I separate the two: I agree when the evidence moves me, not to keep the peace. Here I asked to see the real trainer complaints precisely so the decision rested on something external to both of us. If the data had shown streaming was the blocker, I'd have held my ground and said so. Agreeing without that check is just conflict-avoidance dressed up as collaboration.

followUps.q: What do you do now to get this kind of feedback earlier?
followUps.a: I ask for it deliberately rather than waiting. At JPMorgan, before I go deep on an agent feature, I check the sequencing with the ticket authors and the engineers who'll rely on it, framed as 'what's actually blocking you right now'. That surfaces priority mismatches before I've sunk effort in — exactly the mistake I made at Al-Shala when I polished streaming while booking was broken.
